title: Vector Basics
text:
NOTE: First class! _
Function \(f(x)\) -> inputs to outputs, points (ordered pairs) on a coordinate plane

These points can be expressed using vectors

Function \(f(x, y)\) -> ordered triples on a coordinate space

Generally to graph, we need to draw 3D projections onto 2D
RH rule coord system setup:

X/Y are on the horizontal plane (coming out of the page)
X axis as the one coming out of the page to you (as opposed to Y which you might think)
3D space: asymmetry if we swap axes (can’t rotate through 4D)! We need some reference that is asymmetric in all three dimensions.
Index finger +x, Middle finger +y, then thumb points +z.


General vector rules:

\(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{s}\) => multiply components, sum together products
\(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\) => add components
Vector has no “position”, only a displacement, with direction!
Famous parallelogram rule for sum of vectors in standard position
Subtraction: A - B = vector from B, to A
||v|| = sqrt(sum(vi**2))
3+D spaces, you can only find angle between vectors! (you can’t get angle info from single components)
u = ||u|| * <cos(alpha), cos(beta), cos(gamma)> (THIS IS ACTUALLY THE UNIT VECTOR !!!!)

title: 15.6 Tangent Planes and Linear Approximation
text:
Finding the tangent plane to a surface \(f(x, y, z)=0\) At the point \((a, b, c...)\) \[
\boxed{f_x(a, b, c...)(x-a) + f_y(a, b, c...)(y-b) + f_z(a, b, c...)(z-c)... = 0}
\] I don’t know how to derive this neither do I want to \(f_x\), \(f_y\), \(f_z\) etc are partials
Surface \(z\) at \((a, b, f(a,b))\): \(z = f_x(a, b)(x-a) + f_y(a, b)(y-b) + f(a, b)\)
Linear approximation of \(f(x, y)\) at \((x_1, y_1)\) Create the tangent plane, and plug in values for \((x_1, y_1)\) - Similar to 2D Calculus
Approximating \(dz\) You simply use \(\Delta x \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + \Delta y \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}...\)

title: 616c616e
text:
\(f_x = f_y = 0\) critical point! \(f_x\) or \(f_y\) does not exist -> critical point!
How do we find the local minima/maxima on a surface \(f(x, y)\)?

Review: properties of local maxima/minima

Bigger/smaller than surrounding values
Note that tangent plane is 0, and it is in fact where it changes sign

Maxima: positive slope before, negative after
Minima: negative slope before, positive after

What about absolute maxima?

They must either be also local maxima, or else must be end behavior of the function.

Tangent plane flat, what does that mean?

clearly partials in \(x\) and \(y\) must both be zero
gradient \(\nabla\) must be 0
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{f_x}{f_y}\)
which is just \(-\dfrac{(\nabla f)_x}{(\nabla f)_y}\) (keep in mind the subscript here is components of a vector, not partial derivatives) -> neat to keep in mind


So, an initial naive technique for finding such local maxima/minima could be as follows:

Find some \(x\) s.t. \(f_x=0\) and \(x\) is a local maxima/minima along \(x\) axis; using \(f_x\), find constraints on possible values of \(y\)
At an above value \(y\), test to make sure it’s also a maxima/minima along \(y\) axis, and reconcile the constraint on \(x\)
What about a saddle point? Consider the middle of a hyperbolic paraboloid:

Loc. minimum along one axis, loc. max along the other!!!
How do we deal with this???


Improving this:

Set \(f_x=f_y=0\), solve for \((x, y, f)\) -> critical points
It turns out that concavity tests in one variable (using the second derivative, i.e. \(f''(x)\)) also scale to multiple variables!

For any given critical point \((x_c, y_c)\), \(f_{xx}\) and \(f_{yy}\) must be nonzero (otherwise these are inflections along \(x\) or \(y\) axes!) and have the same sign.


So, for a determinant \(D \coloneqq f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}f_{yx}\) at a given point \((x, y, f)\), we can try a determinant test for well-behaving, twice-differentiable functions:

But remember Clairaut’s theorem for well-behaving functions: \(f_{xy}=f_{yx}\)!
Thus we have \(D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2\)
The determinant test states the following:

If \(D > 0\):

\(f_{xx} > 0 \implies \text{local }\textbf{minimum}\)
\(f_{xx} < 0 \implies \text{local }\textbf{maximum}\)

If \(D < 0\): we have a saddle point.
If \(D=0\), the test is inconclusive.


For absolute minima/maxima: it works the same as in 2D too!

Once we find critical points as above, we can survey the area immediately around the other (e.g. \(y \coloneqq y_c\), \(x\in \left[x-c, x+c\right]\) for some specified \(c\)) to check appropriate concavity

title: 15.8 Lagrange Multipliers
text:
Project object onto surface? ! Please note that notes from 15.4-15.6 haven’t been made yet, some stuff may need linking in here

Main Question:
Find the abs min/max of \(f(x, y)\) subject to a constraint, \(g(x, y)\) - \(g(x, y)\) is like a level curve, at \(z = 0 = g(x,y)\)


Defining stuff
Let \(g\) represent the curve that is represented by the intersection of \(z=0\) and \(g(x, y)\) \(\nabla f\) - the gradient of \(f\), the direction at which \(f\) increases the most, projected onto the \(x\)-\(y\) plane \(\nabla g\) - the gradient of \(g\), the direction at which the ==boundary surface== increases the most (projected in \(x\)-\(y\)) - The boundary is given as a surface to aid in finding the normal to the ==boundary curve==


Visualizing what the gradient means
If we make a topographical map of \(f\), by taking the level curve of \(f\) at a certain interval, the gradient vectors of the corresponding \(z\) value would always be normal to the level curve. - The gradient vectors are always normal to the [[15.1 Graphs and Level Curves|level curve]] at the same \(z\) value because you’re trying to minimize the distance to the next [[15.1 Graphs and Level Curves|level curve]] at \(z+dz\) , which is a straight line directly away, directly, hence normal. - By following these gradient vectors of \(f\) at \(z\) through different slices of \(f\) you will eventually reach an extrema


How are gradients used to find the extrema
However we are constrained by \(g(x, y)=0\) (the ==boundary curve==), which, coincidentally, we also have the normal vectors to. As you follow the gradient vectors of \(f\) and eventually reach the edge of the ==boundary curve== without turning back into the boundary afterwards, you have reached a local extrema! - At this point, because it is a local extrema, that means that locally, at this \(z\) value, the boundary curve and the level curve at the same \(z\) value will share the same tangent - The fact that they share the same tangent, means that their normals, the ==gradient vectors==, will be pointing in the same direction. - See [[Gradient & Boundary Curve.excalidraw]] for a diagram where the ==boundary curve== only intersects once with the [[15.1 Graphs and Level Curves|level curve]]


Working backwards for a formula to find extrema
Taking this logic backwards, to find the local extrema of a function \(f(x, y)\) constrained by a level curve of \(g(x, y)\) at \(0\) (or technically any value, but for simplicity \(0\)), we simply search for when \(\nabla f\) is the same direction of \(\nabla g\) => \(\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g\) - The ration of \(\nabla f\) and \(\nabla g\) is \(\lambda\) which is called the ==Lagrange Multiplier== - there is not really a physical use for this, it’s just a useful number in math. - ~={red}[!] There still may be extrema WITHIN the constraint region, which can be found normally by setting \(f_x(x, y)\) and \(f_y(x, y)\), the partials, to \(0\) which ensures that the tangent at that point is a flat plane (similar to Calc BC optimization)=~ -> [[15.7 Optimizing Multivariable Functions|More explanation]]
You may refer to this hand-drawn explanation below ![[Lagrange Multiplier.png]]

title: 15.5 Directional Derivatives and the Gradient
text:
Gradient of a function \(f(x, y)\): The gradient of a 3d function reduces to a 2d vector \(
abla f(x, y) = \langle  rac{\partial f}{\partial x},  rac{\partial f}{\partial y} angle\) This gives the direction of steepest ascent, or maximum \(dz\) The direction of maximum descent is the negative of this vector
Directional derivative of a function \(f\) at \((x_1, y_1)\) towards \(\langle x_2, y_2 angle\) Make sure to use the unit vector of the direction vector \(
abla f(x, y)(x_1, y_1) \cdot \langle x_2, y_2 angle\) For direction of no change, the directional derivative = 0, which means the dot of gradient and direction vector = 0, which means just a vector orthogonal to the gradient vector
The gradient vector at \((x, y)\) is orthogonal to the derivative at the same point \( rac{dy}{dx} = - rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial x}}{ rac{\partial}{\partial y}}\) \(
abla f = \langle  rac{\partial}{\partial x},  rac{\partial}{\partial y} angle\) happens to be the inverse negative of what would’ve been \(dy\) and \(dx\) for slope, \( rac{dy}{dx}\)

text: Some berries I found today, I want to try to germinate them but it doesn’t seem like there’s a lot of information online about them. There does seem to be some strange wool or fur on the berries…

title: Hillside Gooseberry
text:
Some basic info…
This plant does appear in the calscape database, and it’s native to California so it’s most likely beneficial to plant this for the environment. The bush was originally found near a creek in a partially shady area, but the Wikipedia page does list this plant as belonging to chaparral communities. Also as I’m writing this, it seems like the Wikipedia page has a dead link to USDA’s database. Fixing that…
The bush also contains a decent amount of thorns and I was pricked quite a bit by them, and it’s pretty evident from the berries as well. Also, most berries need cold stratification, however I’m not completely sure about this.
Some more information to note that may be useful as reference for anybody who wants to find this plant though:

The berries ripen around May in my coastal CA region
They are quite prickly, so careful when trying to collect berries
Usually found in partially shady areas, as undergrowth

CNPS (California Native Plant Society, cool organization!) has a page about native plant propagation, it also happens to include this plant! I do hear that most berries like these include chemical inhibitors within the pulp to prevent germination, so to ensure they only germinate after being ingested by an animal. They name a method of fermenting the mashed pulp before germination for another Ribes species, so I will be attempting that for these berries I have. Apparently the mashing/fermenting simulates passage through the digestive system, to remove the inhibiting chemicals.
I’m not certain about the need for cold stratification though, so I will try half in the refrigerator for a week, and another half directly in pots outdoors with consistent moisture (it’s currently May, and I’m in around USDA zone 9b. I think this is enough to start trying to propagate this plant, lets get to preparing!
For my germination procedure:

Mash and ferment the berries for around a week
Clean berries of pulp
Place half of the beries on wet paper towel in the fridge for a week, then also plant in that compost mix
Place other half in a compost-sand mix outdoors
Water and hope they grow

title: August 2026 Jane Street Puzzle
text:
Original puzzle
First, how can Andy the ant notice he’s in a different place than before? Let’s mark the possible paths on the new hexagon tesselation (white hexagons only), where Andy expects to return home, but doesn’t.
(insert image)
We notice that this pattern has radial symmetry thrice, so we can simplify it to just a home node connected to six hexagons in a loop. Because all the nodes outside this area Andy would discover he’s no longer on his truncated tetrahedron, let’s compute the probability that Andy remains inside this loop.
(insert image of hexagon loop)
All of the valid paths that remain inside this loop should start and end at Andy’s home node at the bottom, so we can safely just eliminate the first and last node. Andy can also only have more than 3 nodes in total (so one node other than the homes), otherwise he’d be going nowhere. In addition, we also notice that couting every single node Andy visits, we cannot have odd numbers. Andy can always turn back on his path, in which he visits every node but the tip an even number of times (so 2n + 1, odd), or he goes full circle, in which he visits six nodes, but the one adjacent to his home node twice. Again, this is odd. Any combination of these nodes result in an odd number greater than or equal to one after excluding home.
(insert image showing possible paths)
I then attempted to simplify the problem, noticing that almost every node had 2 of 3 nodes being valid nodes, except for home and the one adjacent to home. I proceeded to try to compute an infinite sum as N approaches infinity, of the sorts: \[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}{(\frac{2}{3})^{2n+1}}
\] I was thinking that for each node that’s not home, he’d have a 2/3 chance of staying, so for a path of length n, we’d have a (2/3)^n chance of staying on the valid nodes. However, I was wrong since we need to determine the weights for having a path of length n. How many ways can we have Andy walk 5 non-home nodes? or 7? I realized that this would be extremely difficult to define, and we still must distinguish between each node, as they each have a different distance from home. Through just an infinite sum I’d have no way to distinguish different ways of terminating a path.
Thus, after doing some research on graph walks, I realized that Markov Chains are actually frequently used to represent these, with states being the nodes that Andy is currently on, and the output space of the Markov Matrix being the probabilities that given Andy is on this node (or on a probability distribution of some nodes), what’s the probability of visiting the other nodes.
(markov diagram with rows and cols labels)
I also learnt about the concept of absorbing states. If Andy has returned home, we don’t care about anything, because he stays home. So if Andy is in the “home” state in the markov chain, we pay no attention, and just assign 1 to “home” in the output, and zero to everything else. Otherwise, if Andy has left the space and realized that he’s no longer on his tetrahedron, he can’t simply un-realize and step back into the valid segment of the graph. Thus in our problem, there’s two of these absorbing states: “home” and “outside.”
When we try to find the tendency of a markov decision process as the evolution tends to infinity (which we want, since the absorbing states automatically “terminate” the evolution and whenever andy hits an absorbing state he stays there), from some basic linear algebra, we know to find the eigenvecters. The dominant eigenvector would have an eigenvalue of 1, since if it was less than one (like the other eigenvectors), it would tend towards zero and evolve-out. If it was greater than one, a probability > 1 doesn’t make sense.
I was thinking, something must be off. How do we represent the initial state? We set home to be an absorbing state, and dropped starting from home, so how do we represent Andy leaving home? Evolving from any other state vector wouldn’t make sense since we know Andy always starts from the home hexagon. Let’s pause here and note for a second that the state vector is actually probabilities that sum up to one. Ok, let’s move on now.
Let’s call our markov chain matrix \(A\), and any initial vector \(v\). we know that as we evolve this process \(n\) times, we approach a resultant vector \(A^n \cdot v\). And this always tends towards an eigenvector. Wait, eigenvector, right? Don’t we already know it? Since the “home” state vector multiplied by the matrix \(A\) is just the same vector, and also the “outside” state vector is just the same vector too… They also happen to be orthogonal as in their dot products equal zero.
This means that for eigenvalue \(\lambda=1\), we actually have two valid eigenvectors representing each absorbing state. Referencing this math stackexchange post, if we put everything in \(A\)’s eigenvector basis, including our starting condition (which is actually not the home node, but one step after so we don’t get immediately trapped in the home condition), we notice that there are two eigenvectors that remain with an eigenvalue of one. The matrix is also diagonalizable (as we see later on, the eigenvector basis is complete), so we know we can write the initial state vector \(v_0\) as a linear combination of the eigenvectors. note that the eigenvectors aren’t necessarily all mutually orthogonal, so even though the dot product between \(v_0\) and the vectors for “home” and “out” are zero, there is still some coefficient.
Why linear combinations though? I’m stuck. Hm. Let’s think about \(lim_{n -> \infty}(A^n \cdot v_0)=v_f\). If we decompose \(A^n \cdot v_0\) into \(PD^n P^{-1} \cdot v_0\), we can simplify the exponentiation by diagonalizing the matrix. For some quick intuition of why we can diagonalize a matrix like this, “eigen” is German for “own”, meaning that each matrix has it’s own unique eigenvectors and eigenvalues. This means uisng the eigenvectors and eigenvalues somehow, you can uniquely specify a matrix. Or, you can think of it like rewriting it, stretching it along the eigenvalues as appropriate, then throwing it back to the old basis.
As \(n\) approaches infinity, we notice that all the eigenvalues less than one decay to zero (since we just exponentiate the diagonal values for diagonal matrices), and the ones equal to one stay. So for our case, \(D^n\) becomes a diagonal matrix with ones for the eigenvectors representing “home” and “outside”. \(P^{-1}\) is a change of basis to rewrite \(v_0\) in the eigenvector basis, then we select the coefficients for the eigenvectors of “home” and “outside”, and \(P\) puts it back into the standard basis. We can do \(D^\infty\) really easily since it’s just a diagonal matrix with some ones and some less than ones. We notice that the diagonal for \(D^\infty\) results in zeros for everything other than the “home” and “outside” eigenvectors. This is basically the same thing in the stackexchange post where a user says that all non-one eigenvalue eigenvectors disappear from the rewriting in the eigenvector basis.
Onto solving this problem, here’s just some busy work computing the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A\), and multiplying through \(PD^{\infty}P^{-1} \cdot v_0\). We notice that all this complexity arises from having multiple dominant eigenvectors, and not just one. If we trace back our logic to solving the problem, we notice it originates from this problem having two “absorbing states”, which introduces two eigenvectors with eigenvalues of both one. Otherwise, the steady state vector would just be the (presumedly otherwise) single eigenvector.
(Ooops I made my matrix row-stochastic but used column-stochastic conventions…)
import sympy

third = sympy.Rational(1, 3)

matrix = sympy.Matrix([
    [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0],
    [third, 0, third, 0, 0, 0, third, 0],
    [0, third, 0, third, 0, 0, 0, third],
    [0, 0, third, 0, third, 0, 0, third],
    [0, 0, 0, third, 0, third, 0, third],
    [0, 0, 0, 0, third, 0, third, third],
    [0, third, 0, 0, 0, third, 0, third],
    [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]
]).transpose()

sympy.pprint(matrix)

P, D = matrix.diagonalize()

vinit = sympy.Matrix([
[0],
[1],
[0],
[0],
[0],
[0],
[0],
[0]
])

D_inf = D.applyfunc(lambda x: 1 if x == 1 else 0)

sympy.pprint(P * D_inf * P.inv() * vinit)
If you think about it abstractly though… this is sort of comparing a \(K_4\) graph to the new graph on the giant infinite tiled floor. Quite an interesting problem if you think about it. Other than that, I think I should’ve paid attention more in linear algebra, or put more rigor in myself…

title: Deep Learning IO Games
text: I got bored, so what if I tasked myself to make a neural network play a 2d battle royale shooter game? So for the basics, survev is just a clone of the original surviv.io, where you basically just play 5 ish minutes games against other players, wanting to be the last one alive. It seems simple enough, with the inputs just being mouse aim, wasd, and some other keys.

title: Deep Learning IO Games
section: Let’s start with the game interface:
text:
Let’s start with the game interface:
I decided to use selenium so I have built in screen capture methods, and also direct input control without the complexity of hooking into the game, and also without too much overhead. I initially used the built in driver.get_screenshot_as_png() method to take screenshots of the game for the neural network, but it was a bit slow, and I discovered that you could directly interface with the chrome dev tools to capture a screenshot faster, with driver.execute_cdp_cmd("Page.captureScreenshot", {...args})
Anyways with all of that key_down and key_up coding overhead over with, I was deciding between different input representations. One side, I would have which keys are being held down for movement and interaction, then another I’d have the cursor position. These were really different data types, as keys being held down was just a boolean state while the cursor was a vector/array of x and y coordinates.
I decided to separate it like the internal game data does, boolean 0s and 1s for keys being held down, but an additional value being whether or not to move the mouse. Then I’d have a separate input for moving the mouse when applicable, if the move enumeration of the keys was set to 1.

title: Deep Learning IO Games
text:
Neural network “heads”?
I’m still pretty clueless about how this works, and I’m just going to play around with the different values, but a large part of this I did use an llm to make… There were two different outputs from the neural network that I was seeking to get: one array of binary states, and another vector of two values from 0-1 (ratio of the screen the cursor is at).
I thought of each neural network as just a large matrix operation, the general gist I’ve always been told. With different layers in this neural network, I thought of the segmentation between the “backbone” of the neural network and each “head.” If the backbone is shared between all the “heads,” naturally each “head” would operate on the same backbone. If each layer was just a different abstraction of the data, then the backbone being the closest to the raw image data would be the main percieving element of the neural network. On this data, each head could independently decide on different output forms.
I had one head dedicated to a boolean state output of 21 something keys, and then I had a vector of two numbers between 0-1. Each head takes in an input of the base backbone CNN, and makes predictions based off of that.

title: Deep Learning IO Games
text:
Initial configuration
I have it set on the torch Adam optimizer, with:
lr = 3e-4
n_steps = 2048
n_epochs = 4
batch_size = 64
gamma = 0.99
gae_lambda = 0.95
clip_eps = 0.2
value_coeff = 0.5
entropy_coeff = 0.01
max_grad_norm = 0.5
step_time = 0.2
while the reward function looks like +0.1 if the bot is alive, +10 for each kill, and 0.1 for each health point change (negative for losing health, positive for healing). When the bot dies, it is peanlized by up to -20, and for each kill it gets, it has a penalty reduction of 2 up to 15. If the bot wins, it gets a +100 reward.
I’m just going to play around with these values for now, and once we get a good amount of steps and eps in, I’ll consider tweaking it around and learning what everything means better while I go.

title: Deep Learning IO Games
Deep Learning IO Games
text:

title: 14.5 Curvature and Normal Vectors
text:
[[Tangents & Normals.excalidraw|Tangents & Normals]]
Unit Tangent Represents the direction in which the particle represented by \(r(t)\) is traveling \(\vec{T}(t)=\frac{\vec{r}'(t)}{||\vec{r}'(t)||}\)
Unit Normal Represents the direction in which the curve represented by \(r(t)\) is curving towards \(\vec{N}(t)=\frac{\vec{T}'(t)}{||\vec{T}'(t)||}\) ### [[Tangential & Normal Acceleration.excalidraw|Acceleration]] \(A=r''(t)\) Obviously \(A_N=\vec{proj}_N A\) and \(A_T=\vec{proj}_T A\) This makes a triangle, with A being the hypotenuse Alternatively, you could use a formula for \(A_T\) and use Pythagorean to find \(A_N\) \(A_T=\frac{d}{dt}||\vec{v}(t)||\) \(A_N=\sqrt{A^2-A_T^2}\)


Curvature & Radius of Curvature
Curvature is represented by \(\kappa\) kappa \(\kappa = \frac{||\vec{T}'(t)||}{v(t)} = \frac{||\vec{v}(t) \times \vec{a}(t)||}{(v(t))^3}\) where \(\vec{v}(t)\) is a vector (velocity) and \(v(t)\) is scalar (speed) The radius of acceleration, \(r\) is simply \(\frac{1}{\kappa}\) The circle of curvature is \(r\) (radius of curvature) away from \(\vec{r}(t)\) in the \(\vec{N}(t)\) direction. \(\vec{N}(t)\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{v}(t)\)


Misc
Projection Drops a vector down to another vector, like dropping down the hypotenuse to a side in a right triangle \(\vec{proj}_v a=\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{v}}{||v||\cdot ||v||}\vec{v}\) Torsion (\(\tau\)) The speed at which \(\vec{r}(t)\) rotates around \(\vec{B}(t)\) \(\tau(t) = -\vec{N}(t) \cdot \vec{B}'(t)\)

title: 15.1 Graphs and Level Curves
text:
Level curves - a family of surfaces related to a function

Let \(z = f(x, y)\) then the level curve at \(z=0\) would be whatever \(0=f(x, y)\) simplifies to.

title: 15.2 Limits and Continuity
text:
Limits

Instead of intervals on each var getting smaller (\(\epsilon\), \(\delta\) proof), use circles.

for \(z=c \pm \delta\), lim \((x, y)\) to \((a, b)\), \((x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 \leq \epsilon\), letting \(\delta := \sqrt{\epsilon}\)

Approaching is no longer along just \(+\) or \(-\) – we can approach from not just any direction, but any curve!

Appraching along \(y=g(x)\) then means adapting \(f(x, y)\) to \(f(x, g(x))\) and then taking a limit. Vice versa.



Weird stuff

Say \(\lim_\limits{(x,y)\to(0,0)} \dfrac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}\) – if we approach along \(x=0\): limit \(0\). Same for any \(y=mx\).

Intuitively, is the limit then \(0\)? – No!

Say we approach along \(y=x^2\) –> lim = \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)!
“Take the limit of \(f(x, y)\) along the left side of \(y=g(x)\)”

title: 15.3 Partial Derivatives
text:
The Derivative

Slope of the tangent line, do you remember our “typical” definition? \[
\lim_\limits{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
\]
But our lim def is weird; how can we possibly find this tangent line?

A: Partial derivatives. ###### Partial derivatives

Suppose that we take a slice along a constant value of \(x\) or \(y\) -> then we can find the tangent line of the cross-section along this plane!

Thus, in (e.g.) \(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\), we’re taking \(\dfrac{dz}{dx}\) along a fixed slice \(y=c\).
Operator wrapping: obviously \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\) -> evaluate the \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\) first.

Consider function \(z=f(x, y)\) where \(x(t)\), \(y(t)\).

We can find \(\dfrac{df}{dt}\):

Method 1: Replace all terms with respective functions of \(t\).
We can also use chain rule!

\(\boxed{\dfrac{df}{dt}=\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt}+\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}\cdot\dfrac{dy}{dt}}\)

This causes the product rule: \(f(x,y)=x^ny^m\implies\dfrac{df}{dt}=nx^{n-1}x'y+mxy^{m-1}y'\)
Extension works too, Df/Dx Dx/Dt dt/dv + … (permute it all out) -> tree it out, each leaf ends with d/dk for ultimate differential variable \(k\).





Directional Derivatives
Taking a derivative of the surface along a unit direction vector \(\overrightarrow{u}\). - Formally: - Rather than doing limit on \(f(a+h, b)-f(a, b)\) and so on, the increment of \(h\) is along \(\overrightarrow{u}\) - \(\left\langle{}a,b\right\rangle{}+h\left\langle{}u_1,u_2\right\rangle\) for \(||\overrightarrow{u}||=1\). - \(\boxed{\lim_\limits{h\to0}\dfrac{f(a+hu_1,b+hu_2)-f(a,b)}{h}}\) - For \(\partial{x}\), \(\overrightarrow{u}=\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle\), and etc. - Simplify the limit: - Let \(g(h)\coloneqq f(a+hu_1, b+hu_2)\) - Limit goes to: \(\lim_\limits{h\to0}\dfrac{g(0+h)-g(0)}{h}\) - Which is \(g'(0)\)… - Which is \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial (x\coloneqq a+hu_1)}u_1 + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial (y\coloneqq b+hu_2)}u_2\)… - Which then simplifies to \(\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right\rangle \cdot \left(\overrightarrow{u}\coloneqq \left\langle \cos{\theta}, \sin{\theta} \right\rangle\right)\)!! - Thus: \[
          \boxed{D_{\overrightarrow{u}}f=\nabla_{x, y}f\cdot\overrightarrow{u}}
          \] - (Note: the gradient operator \(\nabla_{x, y}\) is \(\left\langle \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \right\rangle\), so \(\nabla_{x, y}f\) just means \(\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right\rangle\).) – direction of greatest increase/decrease.

title: 15.4 The Chain Rule
text: Pretty similar to normal chain rule

title: 15.4 The Chain Rule
text:
Partial Chain Rule
Let \(f(x, y) = z\) be a function in terms of \(x\) and \(y\) Let \(x\) be a function of \(s\) and \(t\) Let \(y\) be a function of \(s\) and \(t\)
Then, \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}\) would be \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}\) \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}\) would be the same thing, but instead of the partials of \(x\) and \(y\) in relation to \(s\), it would be in relation to \(t\).

title: 15.4 The Chain Rule
text:
Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) when there’s \(z\)
Let \(z\) be a function of \(x\) and \(y\) Using the partials of \(z\) in terms vof \(x\) and \(y\): \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) would be \(-\frac{\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}}{\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}}\)or, \(-\frac{f_x}{f_y}\)

title: 15.4 The Chain Rule
text:
Partial 2nd derivative Chain Rule
Let \(z\) be a differentiable function of \(x\) and \(y\) Let \(x\) and \(y\) be differentiable functions of \(s\) and \(t\) Then: \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}\) And: \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\) The second derivatives are \(f_{ss}\), \(f_{st}\), and \(f_{tt}\) From the previous formulas: \(f_s = f_x x_s + f_y y_s\) \(f_t = f_x x_t + f_y y_t\) \(f_{ss}\) would be \((f_x x_s + f_y y_s)_s\) \(= (f_x)_s x_s + f_x x_{ss} + (f_y)_s y_s + f_y y_{ss}\) \(\boxed{= (f_{xx}x_s + f_{xy}y_s)x_s + f_x x_{ss} + (f_{yx}x_s + f_{yy} y_s)y_s + f_y y_{ss}}\) You could simplify that, but the grouping makes sense. Simply find these and plug: \(f_x\) \(f_{xy}\) \(f_{xx}\) \(f_y\) \(f_{yx}\) \(f_{yy}\) \(x_s\) \(x_{ss}\) \(y_s\) \(y_{ss}\) Deriving for \(f_{st}\) or \(f_{tt}\) would be a similar process

title: Past Problems: 2025
text:
Definitions:

\(gcd(m_k, n_k) = 1\)
\(\frac{m_k}{n_k} = \frac{2m_{k-1} + 1}{2n_{k-1} + 1}\)
\(m_0, n_0 \in \mathbf{Z}^+\)

The crux of the problem is to prove that \(gcd(2m_k + 1, 2n_k + 1) \neq 1\) for only a finite amount of \(k\)
We may hypothesize (for the sake of contradiction) that the \(gcd \neq 1\) for infinitely many \(k\). Thus in an attempt to prove this, we can set up an inductive hypothesis that if \(gcd(2m_k + 1, 2n_k + 1) \neq 1\), then for \(k+1\) the \(gcd\) is also not \(1\). By dichotomy as well, \(gcd \neq 1\) for infinitely many \(k\)’s XOR finitely many \(k\)’s.
We may

attempt to disprove the inductive hypothesis
attempt to disprove the inductive base case

However attempting to disprove the inductive base case would be trying to prove the nonexistence of a \(gcd \neq 1\) which is stronger than simply proving the finiteness of \(gcd \neq 1\), which I don’t think the problem write would make us do. So we will attempt to disprove the inductive hypothesis, which proves the finiteness of \(gcd \neq 1\).
